verdicts.trueWording: The chapters at the end are just as significant as
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture fetched with a browser UA; HTML stripped locally, no summarizer. Answer to 'What makes a fantasy epic?': she names The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, then the quoted sentence, which ends 'the moment in which the Ring is tossed' - the claim's 'destroyed' is a paraphrase of 'tossed'.

verdicts.trueWording: the familiar is what invites the reader in and makes
verdicts.note: Answer on the blend of strange and familiar. Full sentence opens 'When we blend the strange into a story' and closes 'real to him or her', so both limbs of the claim are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: You know the car, the cereal on the table
verdicts.note: Same answer, illustrating Stephen King. Continues with the cartoon on the tv, then the Bogey-man stepping into your own real world; claim's 'television' renders the page's 'tv'.

verdicts.trueWording: the author has to stop making judgments and let the
verdicts.note: Answer on how her writing has evolved. Preceded by 'And when you write from the character's POV', closed by 'let the character talk', then the Kennit example. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: sacrificing a lot of plot and character words to world-building
verdicts.note: Answer on how the genre has changed. The contrast limb is explicit: 'That's fine if you are writing in our real world, but if you are setting up a fantasy world...'.

verdicts.trueWording: I don't think about foreshadowing or symbolism or themes
verdicts.note: Answer on thematic underpinning; page uses a curly apostrophe in 'don't', matched after normalisation. Preceded by 'I write stories.' and followed by someone cleverer attaching all that afterwards, which supports the 'while writing' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: So I live in a mostly blue-collar world
verdicts.note: Answer on quirks. The attribution limb rests on the next sentence, which is HEDGED - 'Maybe that's why a lot of my characters come from there' - so the claim's flat 'attributes' is firmer than the page; any downstream use should carry the 'Maybe'.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that this is the only contemporary review of the novel in Interzone
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim in the 'First Fantasies' column (item byte-verified at 441642 bytes; OCR double spaces normalised). The stylistic-patchiness limb is fully supported, but a single issue cannot establish exclusivity across the magazine's run - nothing on the page speaks to 'the only'.

verdicts.trueWording: repetitions, awkwardnesses and bad habits creep in
verdicts.note: Both limbs are in one sentence: patchy 'since Hobb attempts to write in a deliberately literary manner at the start and whenever he thinks about it, though his attempts are often in vain', then the quoted result clause. Column signed Chris Morgan at head and foot.

verdicts.trueWording: an exquisitely poetical phrase which says much of human nature
verdicts.note: Immediately follows the patchiness sentence and is introduced by 'It is all the more surprising, then', which carries the claim's 'even while faulting the style' limb. Page closes the sentence 'in just a few words'.

verdicts.trueWording: entertaining after a slow start, sporadically surprising, sometimes subtle
verdicts.note: Opening paragraph of the Hobb review, describing 'an above-average book'; the page continues 'and very occasionally brilliant', which the claim omits without distorting it.

verdicts.trueWording: It is historically-based fiction with relatively small amounts of fantasy
verdicts.note: Sentence stands on its own at the end of the review's opening paragraph, directly after the 'above-average book' assessment. Verbatim after OCR double-space normalisation.

verdicts.trueWording: of an experienced author from another genre (presumably historical fiction)
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that Morgan inferred this from reading the prose - the review names no basis
verdicts.note: The quoted phrase opens the review verbatim, and the 1995 date and Morgan's belief are supported (he uses 'he' of Hobb throughout, e.g. 'so he has been able to avoid'). But it is stated as a premise - 'Because Robin Hobb is the pseudonym of an experienced author... The Assassin's Apprentice is free of most of the problems that tend to infect first novels' - reasoning FROM the identity to the prose, not from the prose to the identity.

verdicts.trueWording: a sudden descent into melodrama of an almost farcical nature
verdicts.note: Verbatim, and the 'end of the novel' limb is on the page: 'only at the end of the novel is there a sudden descent...', set against praise for credible, cleverly interwoven plot strands.
